extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato / readers of classical political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Plato's descriptive criteria for forms of government and corresponding character-types (oligarchical, democratic, tyrannical) as given in Books VIII–IX of the Republic. Focuses on traits, causal processes, and moral-psychological diagnoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchical temperament and ruling class
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Their adherents, especially the young men of the governing class, are habituated to lead a life of luxury and idleness both of body and mind; they do nothing, and are incapable of resisting either pleasure or pain. They themselves care only for making money, and are as indifferent as the pauper to the cultivation of virtue.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the oligarch’s psychology and social habits (luxury, idleness, money‑getting, indifference to virtue). Used to explain how oligarchy produces rulers and citizens unfit for virtuous governance and susceptible to internal decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy’s origin and institutional form
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Democracy comes into being after the poor have conquered their opponents, slaughtering some and banishing some, while to the remainder they give an equal share of freedom and power; and this is the form of government in which the magistrates are commonly elected by lot.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the political mechanism that creates democracy (popular victory, equal shares of freedom, selection by lot) and frames later behavioral consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic character: freedom, variety, and disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In the first place, are they not free; and is not the city full of freedom and frankness—a man may say and do what he likes?... This, then, seems likely to be the fairest of States, being like an embroidered robe which is spangled with every sort of flower... These and other kindred characteristics are proper to democracy, which is a charming form of government, full of variety and disorder, and dispensing a sort of equality to equals and unequals alike.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Captures democracy’s attractive surface (variety, liberty, equality) together with the diagnosis that such liberty tends to disorder and an indiscriminate equality that undermines civic excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary versus unnecessary pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Are not necessary pleasures those of which we cannot get rid, and of which the satisfaction is a benefit to us?... the desires of which a man may get rid... and in some cases the reverse of good... shall we not be right in saying that all these are unnecessary?’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a moral-psychological criterion to evaluate pleasures: necessary pleasures sustain life/health and are beneficial; unnecessary pleasures (luxuries, excessive condiments, vain desires) are dispensable and harmful to body and soul and to the pursuit of wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process: oligarchical upbringing -> democratic conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A young man raised in oligarchical (miserly) habits, when exposed to refined licentious company and external desires, becomes factional within and is converted into the democratic type—‘the change will begin of the oligarchical principle within him into the democratical’ by allies from without assisting internal desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the internal dynamics by which external fashions and companions overturn earlier disciplined habits; emphasizes factional struggle within the soul between old (restraining) and new (libertine) desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the democratic man
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘He lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour; and sometimes he is lapped in drink and strains of the flute; then he becomes a water‑drinker, and tries to get thin; then he takes a turn at gymnastics... busy with politics... His life has neither law nor order; and this distracted existence he terms joy and bliss and freedom.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists behavioral features of the democratic personality: impulsiveness, variety of pursuits, lack of consistent principle, equal valuation of all pleasures, instability and fluctuation in habits and ambitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy’s extreme equality -> social anarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Equality extended without limit: son equal to father, master equal to scholar, citizen equal to metic, animals ‘ready to burst with liberty’ leading to sensitivity to authority and disregard of laws—‘they will have no one over them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnoses how unchecked equality produces breakdowns in authority and social roles, making the polity vulnerable to disorder and eventual demand for a ruler who will restore order (ushering tyranny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three social classes in democracy: drones, wealthy, and workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy can be divided into (1) drones (many idle, loud leaders), (2) the orderly wealthy class who are most squeezable for resources, and (3) the people who work with their hands (the largest class) who must be fed small rewards to mobilize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the sociological anatomy of democracies in Plato’s account: who gains influence (drones), who gets exploited (wealthy), and who forms the mass base (workers), and how leaders manipulate them with promises/honey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the tyrant: the protector turned tyrant
rubrics_metrics.description: A popular champion (‘protector of the people’) arises, using the mob, false accusations, purges and promises (debt abolition, land distribution) to gain power; by repeated crimes and the request for a bodyguard he transforms into a tyrant—‘the protector of the people is like him... by the favourite method of false accusation he brings them into court and murders them... and then... a tyrant.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lays out the political‑psychological trajectory from populist protector to full tyrant: demagoguery, elimination of rivals, manufactured emergency, and solicitation of armed followers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics of tyrannical consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: When in power the tyrant confiscates sacred treasures, spends resources, lowers taxes temporarily, recruits bodyguards (often freed slaves), impoverishes and taxes the populace, repeatedly wages wars to keep them dependent, and purges the valiant, wise, and wealthy to eliminate threats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides practical steps a tyrant uses to secure and sustain rule: economic confiscation, creation of loyal armed clients, manufacturing external threats, and systematic removal of potential rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyrant’s rule and misery
rubrics_metrics.description: Initially popular and flattering, the tyrant becomes unpopular and must continually create wars and purges; he lives among bad companions, is hated, and requires ever more satellites and devotion—‘the more detestable his actions are to the citizens the more satellites... will he require?’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the moral and psychological condition of the tyrant: outward power coupled with inward insecurity and social isolation; the account evaluates the true (un)happiness of tyrannical life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawless appetites and the need for reason’s vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain unnecessary pleasures are ‘unlawful’; they awaken when ‘the reasoning and human and ruling power is asleep’ and may lead to incest, parricide, and other extreme crimes. To avoid this one must ‘awaken his rational powers... feed them on noble thoughts...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prescriptive psychological rule: reason must be cultivated and roused (e.g., before sleep) to keep irrational appetites from overrunning the soul; practical example given is meditative instruction prior to sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of the tyrannical man from democratic stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic man’s son, exposed to libertine life, is induced to acquire a single master passion (a ‘monstrous winged drone,’ often love) which rules the soul; thereafter madness leads him to spend, incur debts, plunder, and even tyrannize over parents—thus the tyrannical man is formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological developmental account: a dominant passion supplants other parts of the soul, producing frenzy and immoral action. Examples: feasts, courtesans, mounting debts, deception, force, and parricide as possible outcomes.
